selected_mechanism.name: FERC non-capacity license amendment on the delegated-authority track, Bradley Lake Expansion / Dixon Diversion, Project No. P-8221-124
selected_mechanism.one_line_definition: The Federal Power Act process by which an existing hydro licensee amends its license without adding meaningful nameplate capacity. Because 18 CFR 375.308(b) lets a single delegated FERC officer act on uncontested amendment applications, the 5:00 p.m. ET 2026-08-28 intervention deadline is the hour that decides whether a 38 percent increase in the output of Alaska's largest hydro plant is disposed of by one officer or by a contested Commission proceeding.

news_trigger.verbatim_quote: The licensee proposes to: (1) build a new diversion dam to divert meltwater and surface runoff coming from the Dixon Glacier, located at the headwaters of the Martin River, into Bradley Lake; (2) raise the normal maximum operating pool elevation of Bradley Lake by about 16 feet through a combination of raising the concrete spillway crest elevation, adding spillway crest gates, and raising the dam embankment crest; and (3) install a 0.3-megawatt (MW) micro-hydro turbine in one of the Bradley Lake Dam's fishwater release valves.
news_trigger.outlet: Federal Register (FERC notice, FR Doc. 2026-15691), via govinfo.gov
news_trigger.supporting_verbatim_deadline: Deadline for filing comments, motions to intervene, and protests: August 28, 2026 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time
news_trigger.supporting_verbatim_output: average annual power generation by approximately 38 percent
news_trigger.supporting_verbatim_standing: only those who file a motion to intervene in accordance with the Commission's Rules may become a party to the proceeding

layers.name: Delegated-disposition layer (CHOKEPOINT)
layers.what_it_does: Standing Commission regulation delegates to one officer the power to act on uncontested amendment applications under Part I of the Federal Power Act. Whether this 400 million dollar amendment stays on that one-officer track or leaves it is decided entirely by whether any protest or intervention is on file when the 2026-08-28 clock runs out.
layers.controlling_actor: Director, FERC Office of Energy Projects, or the Director's designee, acting under delegated authority in 18 CFR 375.308(b)(1)

primary_source.outlet: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School (18 CFR 375.308)

It is the body through which the amendment's physical and cost consequences reach the five purchaser utilities that resell the power.

chokepoint.layer: Delegated-disposition layer (18 CFR 375.308(b)(1)), gated by the 2026-08-28 5:00 p.m. ET intervention deadline set in the acceptance notice
chokepoint.controlling_actor: Director, FERC Office of Energy Projects, or the Director's designee
chokepoint.binary_decision: If no protest or motion to intervene is on file at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on 2026-08-28, the application is uncontested and one delegated officer may take appropriate action on it, including issuing the amending order with conditions. If it is contested, that officer's delegated authority does not reach it.
chokepoint.why_asymmetric: One officer, one binary, inside their own delegated authority, and the switch that arms or disarms that authority is a clock, not a vote. No committee sits between the Director and the order on the uncontested track. The Bradley Lake Project Management Committee, by contrast, is six members and is a governance body, not a chokepoint. The asymmetry is doubled by the standing rule in the same notice: only those who file a motion to intervene may become a party. A party that misses the hour does not merely lose a vote, it loses the ability to contest the terms at all, which is also what keeps the delegated track open.

ak_consequence.sector: Railbelt electric generation and the firm-power headroom underneath any Anchorage- or Fairbanks-interconnected AI compute load
ak_consequence.decision_or_risk: Whether the largest identified block of new firm non-gas Railbelt energy in any regulatory queue, an approximately 38 percent increase in Bradley Lake's average annual power generation, is disposed of on a one-officer delegated track with conditions no Alaska load developer had standing to shape, is fixed at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on 2026-08-28.
ak_consequence.named_actors: Alaska Energy Authority (licensee, FERC Project No. 8221); Director, FERC Office of Energy Projects; the five BPMC purchaser utilities (Chugach, Golden Valley, Homer, Matanuska, Seward Electric); AEA Board of Directors
ak_consequence.timeframe: Intervention deadline 2026-08-28; AEA board returns to final financing terms after Railbelt utility review this fall; per AEA's own schedule, roughly three years of study and permitting followed by three years of construction.

selected_mechanism.structural_read: This is the power gate underneath Alaska AI, not an AI mechanism, and the desk says so plainly. Bradley Lake is the state's largest hydro plant and the amendment would raise its average annual generation by about 38 percent while adding only 0.3 MW of nameplate. That nameplate arithmetic is the whole trick. Because the capacity does not meaningfully move, the project rides the non-capacity amendment track rather than a relicensing, and non-capacity amendments are exactly the class that 18 CFR 375.308(b) hands to a single delegated officer when nobody contests them. So the largest single addition of firm non-gas energy on the Railbelt is, procedurally, a routine amendment. That is not a scandal. It is the ordinary shape of Federal Power Act administration, and it is why the leverage in this mechanism sits in a clock rather than in a hearing. The honest limits: AEA's own page says the construction funding source is yet to be determined, and its own schedule puts first power at the far end of a six-year study-permit-build sequence. Nothing here relieves the Cook Inlet gas problem constraining Railbelt interconnection today, and any pitch that this is near-term capacity for a 2027 or 2028 data center is wrong. What it is, is the one place in the current queue where the terms of Alaska's late-decade firm energy supply are being set, on a docket where the list of people entitled to argue about those terms closes in fourteen days.
selected_mechanism.forward_implication: Any Railbelt-connected load developer, independent power producer, or prospective large-tenant offtaker that expects to negotiate against Bradley Lake energy after 2030 should decide this week whether to file a motion to intervene in FERC Project No. P-8221-124 before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on 2026-08-28. Positioned today: AEA as licensee, the five BPMC purchaser utilities who already sit inside project governance, and the resource agencies. Not positioned: every non-utility load developer and offtaker who is not on the docket, and who after that hour will have no party status and no standing to contest operating conditions, pool-elevation constraints, or the terms that ultimately flow into what they are quoted. Second date to hold: the AEA board's return to final financing terms after Railbelt utility review this fall, where the approximately 400 million dollar cost with a still-undetermined funding source gets assigned.
selected_mechanism.recurrence_note: This gate fires on a per-application basis and has fired three times on this project (draft application 2026-02-13, final application 2026-06-30, acceptance and intervention notice 2026-08-03). The delegated-authority switch in 18 CFR 375.308(b) is standing and recurs on every uncontested FPA Part I amendment nationally. The same FERC hydro machinery opened a second Alaska docket eight days later at Terror Lake (P-2743-112). FERC hydropower licensing has never been mapped by this column and the controlling actor is new to the series.
selected_mechanism.overlap_resolution: The facilities scout and the regulatory scout surfaced the same trigger with different chokepoints. Resolved against the regulatory scout's CWA Section 401 framing and in favor of a sharpened version of the facilities scout's FERC framing, on two grounds. First, sourcing: the 401 layer required asserting that ADEC is Alaska's Section 401 certifying authority for this project, and that could not be confirmed from any fetchable primary source. dec.alaska.gov returns HTTP 403 and EPA's own CWA 401 page defines the certifying-authority power generically without naming any state agency. Neither the Federal Register notice nor AEA's BLEP page mentions Section 401, water quality certification, or ADEC. The 401 layer was dropped rather than asserted, and the chain does not break. Second, on the merits: the facilities scout located the asymmetry in the 2026-08-28 deadline but attributed the binary to the Office of Energy Projects as an office. The verifiable version, which neither scout identified, is 18 CFR 375.308(b)(1), under which the Commission has already delegated to one named officer the authority to act on uncontested amendment applications. The 2026-08-28 hour is the switch that determines whether that one-officer authority applies at all.
